newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Kurds disperse after occupying U.N. in Geneva.
newsitem.headline: Kurds disperse after occupying U.N. in Geneva.

text.p: Kurdish demonstrators ended an occupation of the European headquarters of the United Nations on Thursday after winning a fresh U.N. condemnation of Turkey's incursion into northern Iraq.

The 200 Kurds, whose demands included Security Council action against Ankara, held three hours of negotiations with U.N. officials in Geneva before leaving the premises peacefully, police and U.N. officials said.

U.N. officials defused the potentially violent crisis by reissuing a statement by Secretary General Kofi Annan in which he urged Turkish troops to withdraw "as soon as possible" and called on other governments to pressure Ankara to pull back.

Vladimir Petrovsky, U.N. director-general in Geneva and once a deputy foreign minister of the old Soviet Union, was in telephone contact with Annan in New York during the nearly five-hour crisis, according to some U.N. sources.

"From the beginning, the discussions focussed on ending things peacefully," U.N. spokesman Jamel Ben Yahmed said. "We told them their action was unacceptable. But we have taken note of their demands and are going to transmit them to New York."

Kurdish demands included a U.N. ultimatum to make Turkey withdraw. They also sought an investigation into reports of killings during Turkey's push into northern Iraq, now in its ninth day of a drive against Kurdish separatist guerrillas.

More than 10,000 Turkish troops, allied with the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), poured into northern Iraq last week in pursuit of Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) rebels who use northern Iraq as a base to launch raids into southeast Turkey.
Elif Aktas, spokeswoman for the Kurdish demonstrators, told reporters in German: "Our action has been successful. "This will show that the Kurds should not be ignored."
U.N. officials asked police to come onto its extraterritorial premises, but decided not to give the order to break up the occupation, according to U.N. and police officials.
As soon as the demonstrators left the sprawling Palais des Nations, 150 armed riot police emerged from the building's stairwells and encircled them outside the gates.
Geneva police said they would check their identities, but would let them disperse after about an hour. No arrests were reported.
"Coordination with U.N. security was good. Everything went smoothly and the occupation did not degenerate," Geneva police spokesman Jacques Volery told Reuters.
The only damage was a shattered entrance door as the demonstrators rushed past security guards at the main gate and forced their way into the Palais des Nations.
But some U.N. guards were shaken by the occupation of the 1930s building, which overlooks Lake Geneva and was the original home of the League of Nations.
"Now is not the time to make budget cuts in security," grumbled one of the U.N. security guards, who carry no arms. "We were told to stop them, then not to," complained another.

The Kurds, who were mainly men but included a few women and children, chanted and danced in the austere halls of the complex. They voted to stay there unless the world body passed a resolution condemning the Turkish assault.
"We are demanding action by the United Nations and the international community to halt the massacre of our people in northern Iraq," said one who identified himself as Argun Leman.
"The Turks have killed over 100 civilians, including many women and children. Why is nothing being done to stop them?"
